newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE-German phone giant in Europe's biggest IPO.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-German phone giant in Europe's biggest IPO.

text.p: The first-time sale of shares in telephone giant Deutsche Telekom AG this month is set to become Europe's largest-ever listing, worth some $10 billion, and has whipped up "stock fever" among normally cautious Germans.

When shares begin trading on stock markets around the world on November 18, Telekom's long, gruelling transition from a stodgy state bureaucracy to a dynamic multinational company in one of the fastest-growing industries will come to a close.

As many as 575 million Deutsche Telekom shares, expected to be priced at around 30 marks, will be floated on stock markets in Germany, New York, Tokyo and could eventually be issued in Hong Kong and Singapore and other cities around the globe.
As the deadline for orders from private investors at special discounts arrived on Wednesday, observers predicted the issue could be oversubscribed as much as five times.

"The massive response from private investors, combined with the interest shown by institutional investors, convinces me that the flotation of Deutsche Telekom will be a genuine success," chief executive Ron Sommer said recently.

When Finance Minister Theo Waigel disclosed plans in 1992 to privatise Telekom, he said, "This could become the people's share of the '90s," in a reference to the historic flotations of industry giants Veba AG and Volkswagen AG in the heyday of Germany's post-war economic miracle.
HARD SELL

Telekom resorted to a hard sell with a splashy television advertising campaign using actor Manfred Krug, the German "Columbo" of TV detectives, telling millions of prime-time couch potatoes it would be foolish to miss out on the offer.
The emotional message hit home. More than three million private investors have since shed long-held aversions to the risks of buying shares and registered with Telekom.
"We have succeeded with the marketing surrounding the T-share over the past weeks and months of stirring up real "stock fever" in Germany," said Sommer.

Telekom gave Germans plenty of reasons to get in on the act. Anyone who buys a "T-share" will get a dividend of 60 pfennigs for 1996 and 1.20 marks for 1997. Anyone that keeps shares for three years will get one new share for every ten held. Those who signed up with the company can buy shares at a discount of 50 pfennigs.

More than twice as many Germans signed up for Telekom's IPO than Britons for British Telecom's hugely successful listing 12 years ago. The listing could become the watershed event that Germany has longed for to yank its provincial stock markets onto the international stage. Just 5.5 percent of Germans own shares now, compared to 17.5 percent of Britons and a whopping 21 percent of Americans.
BROADENING SHARE OWNERSHIP BASE
Broadening the base of share ownership would also benefit the economy as a whole and especially young, innovative start-up companies by making it easier to find financing.
"The privatisation of Telekom is good for the whole share market," said Werner Seifert, management board chairman of the German stock exchange holding company, Deutsche Boerse AG.

But the impact of the listing goes beyond Germany. It will probably be the largest-ever listing of a foreign company in Tokyo and the offer is already affecting European telecoms companies. Shares in some European carriers have risen as they are considered undervalued in light of Telekom's IPO price.
And analysts say that a successful Deutsche Telekom flotation could bode well for issues to come later, such as France Telecom, which goes up for sale next year.

Deutsche Telekom's privatisation, some eight years in the making, has also transformed the company from a rigid state bureaucracy with little concern for its customers to a company doing all it can to quickly modernise and hone services.

The government broke up the former postal ministry in 1989 into three agencies -- Deutsche Bundespost Telekom, banking arm Deutsche Bundespost Postbank and post office Deutsche Bundespost. In 1995, they were transformed into joint stock corporations fully-owned by the government.
The Bonn government will continue to hold a majority stake in Deutsche Telekom until the year 2000, the first opportunity it will have by law to sell its shares.

"We want to become the most customer-friendly company on the global telecommunications market so that our customers enjoy working with us and forget about the competition," said chief executive Sommer.

Sommer, a "whiz kid" who received his doctorate in mathematics at the age of 22, started his career at German computer maker Nixdorf and later ran Sony's American and European operations before joining Telekom last year.
The 47-year-old executive has already had a huge impact on the company as he sets out to quietly bring about a shift in corporate culture and prepare the company for competition.
He has filled the management board with outsiders, putting Dutchman Erik Jan Nederkoorn, former head of aircraft maker Fokker NV, in charge of international activities.
COMPETITION POSES GREATER CHALLENGES
But the greatest challenges for Sommer and Deutsche Telekom are yet to come.

Only a small part of the company's activities face competition, areas such as mobile phones and provision of corporate networks. The lion's share of revenues come from services protected by Telekom's 100-year-old monopoly.

But that will all change with the "Big Bang" in 1998, when Europe opens the doors to telecoms competition. And after the listing, industry observers say regulators in Brussels and Washington will step up the pressure on Germany to curtail Telekom's enormous power in the marketplace.

Alliances between big German companies such as engineering group Mannesmann AG, energy group Veba AG, and utilities RWE AG and Viag AG have teamed up with the likes of AT&T, British Telecom and Cable and Wireless to challenge the local giant.

These companies hope to carve out a piece of Germany's telecommunications market for themselves. Valued at around 80 billion marks now, Europe's biggest telecoms market is expected to grow to 100 billion marks a year by 2000.
Hopeful competitors have earmarked a combined investment of over $10 billion to build up competitive networks and services.
"Only powerful alliances with a broad and comprehensive product offering will survive," said Dietmar Kuhnt, head of RWE after joining an alliance of Veba AG and Cable and Wireless.

Facing challenges at home, Telekom is on a global shopping spree, buying stakes in phone companies from Hungary to Malaysia and bids as far away as South Africa. It eventually wants to generate 20 percent of its sales outside Germany.

Telekom has formed a strategic alliance with France Telecom. Previous Telekom executives have said that the German and French phone companies could take stakes in each other when Telekom's second batch of shares is sold off, expected in 1998. Together, the two companies own 20 percent of Sprint Corp of the United States and all three formed the Global One international telecoms venture.

Perhaps the greatest challenge to Telekom is reining in its debt. Analysts have pointed out that totalling over 100 billion marks, Telekom's debt is higher than Turkey's and it is the world's second most-indebted enterprise.

The company must also cut it workforce from a bloated level of 230,000 when it became a joint stock company in 1995 to 170,000 by the end of the century. But that is still too high in some analysts' estimates.
